content: Damage to the structure or function of a nerve is a recognized complication in leprosy, even when the damage is too mild to be clinically measurable. The term neuropathy refers to nerve dysfunction caused by any etiology, while neuritis specifically denotes inflammation of the nerve, often involving the host's immune system. Neuritis is considered the primary mechanism of nerve damage during the acute phase of leprosy. Clinically, the focus is on measurable nerve function, assessed through various methods collectively termed nerve function assessment. Any loss of nerve function is classified as an impairment, specifically referred to as nerve function impairment (NFI). The terminology for impairments and disabilities is standardized in the International Classification of Functioning, Disability, and Health (WHO, 2001). Impairments can lead to activity limitations and social consequences, such as stigma and discrimination, which significantly impact the lives of individuals affected by leprosy. Leprosy reactions are immune-mediated inflammatory episodes that can be self-limiting or severe and prolonged. These reactions are the primary cause of disability in leprosy and contribute to many psychosocial consequences. Two main types of reactions are recognized: Type 1 and Type 2, each with distinct features. Even after leprosy treatment, nerve pain can recur due to various causes, including leprosy relapse, neuropathic pain, or entrapment neuropathy. Entrapment neuropathy occurs when an enlarged nerve becomes compressed in fibro-osseous tunnels, such as the cubital tunnel at the elbow or the carpal tunnel at the wrist, causing pain and functional loss. Splinting may help, but surgery is often required. Leprosy cases present with a wide range of clinical features, classified along a spectrum based on clinical signs, histopathology, immune response, and bacillary load. The Ridley-Jopling classification was simplified by WHO into two groups—paucibacillary (PB) and multibacillary (MB)—for treatment purposes when multidrug therapy (MDT) was introduced in 1981. However, operational definitions for PB/MB classification have changed over time, complicating comparisons of results across different eras. More patients are now classified and treated as MB cases than in the past. Type 1 reactions, also known as reversal reactions, are caused by an inflammatory response to Mycobacterium leprae in tissues, triggered by a sudden alteration in cell-mediated immunity. These reactions may occur as a presenting feature of leprosy, during MDT, or even years after treatment completion. Starting MDT often precipitates a Type 1 reaction, possibly due to the rapid killing of bacilli, which allows the immune system to recover. Typical inflammatory features include swelling, redness, heat, pain, and loss of function. Inflammation around bacilli in skin lesions is the central clinical feature, which is usually self-limiting and resolves over weeks with symptomatic treatment. Severe cases may lead to ulceration of inflamed skin lesions. A more critical issue is that skin reactions are often accompanied by inflammation in one or more nerves (neuritis), which can result in permanent nerve damage, impairment, and disability. Skin reactions, especially on the face, may indicate impending neuritis and require careful monitoring. Reactions are present in approximately 22% of new leprosy cases at diagnosis. Mild reactions without neuritis can be managed with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) like aspirin, ibuprofen, or paracetamol. Regular nerve function assessment is essential for detecting NFI, whether due to overt inflammation or silent neuritis. Early detection of NFI allows for timely steroid treatment, which can reverse nerve damage if initiated within six months. Type 2 reactions, also known as erythema nodosum leprosum (ENL), are multisystem, relapsing, and remitting disorders occurring in patients with lepromatous (LL) or borderline-lepromatous (BL) leprosy and high bacillary loads. ENL is thought to result from circulating immune complexes with widespread systemic effects. The ENLIST consortium, formed in 2014, has significantly advanced the understanding of Type 2 reactions. A Severity Scale was developed to objectively assess and monitor cases. ENL is challenging to treat, requiring careful evaluation of treatment response and disease progression. Management of Type 1 reactions includes both pharmacological and non-pharmacological measures. Resting the affected limb during the acute phase, aided by splinting, is beneficial. Passive stretching and active exercises help preserve joint mobility and strengthen weakened muscles. Soaking and oiling dry skin prevent cracking and maintain epidermal integrity. In some cases, surgery may be necessary to relieve nerve pressure, though this is typically available only in specialist centers. Rehabilitative surgery plays a role in managing permanent nerve damage but is beyond the scope of this discussion. In summary, the clinical management of leprosy reactions and associated nerve damage requires a multidisciplinary approach, including regular nerve function assessments, timely pharmacological interventions, and supportive measures to prevent long-term disability.
